page: Google Cloud Platform g2-standard-48 is a graphics-optimized server featuring 48 vCPUs and 192.0 GB of system memory. The compute architecture is powered by an Intel Xeon processor with 24 physical cores, operating at a base clock speed of 2.2 GHz with hyper-threading enabled. This configuration includes four dedicated NVIDIA L4 GPUs based on the Ada Lovelace architecture, delivering a combined 96 GB of VRAM. There is no local storage bundled with this instance type.

Benchmark results indicate a clear performance split between CPU and GPU tasks. Single-core CPU performance is relatively weak, scoring in the bottom 25% on stress-ng and Geekbench tests, which is also reflected in slower single-threaded compression and decompression speeds. However, multi-core CPU performance and memory bandwidth fall into the average range. In contrast, the GPU-accelerated capabilities are highly competitive, with LLM inference speeds for prompt processing and text generation ranking in the top 10% and top 25% across small, medium, and large models.

From a resource density perspective, the g2-standard-48 offers a balanced allocation of 4.0 GB of RAM per vCPU alongside its quad-GPU setup. The primary tradeoff is the lower single-core CPU performance, meaning workloads heavily reliant on single-threaded CPU execution will experience bottlenecks. However, the high density of NVIDIA L4 GPUs makes this server highly cost-efficient for parallelized, accelerator-dependent workloads. It is optimally suited for large language model inference, machine learning training, graphics rendering, and data science pipelines.

Benchmark data highlights a significant performance divergence: while single-core CPU performance is weak, multi-core capabilities are average, and GPU-driven LLM inference speeds rank in the top tier. This resource profile makes the instance highly efficient for parallel processing tasks. It is best suited for machine learning inference, large language model deployment, and graphics rendering workloads where GPU acceleration offsets the modest single-core CPU performance.
